sections.h2: What rules apply to a Missouri quitclaim deed?
sections.html:
A quitclaim deed is a conveyance of land, so it falls under the same execution and recording rules that Chapter 442 sets for every deed in the state. Missouri statutes name quitclaim deeds directly in a few places, including the offense of filing false documents, which lists a warranty, special or quitclaim deed among the instruments it covers.

Two things decide whether the paper works. It has to be signed and acknowledged the way the statute demands. And it has to be recorded with the recorder of deeds covering the land, in a format the recorder will accept.

Before you sign one, decide whether the transfer is final and whether you are giving up a say in a later sale. Your title company can tell you what it will want to see.

RSMo 442.130 requires every deed or conveyance of land to be subscribed by the person granting it, or by a lawful agent, and acknowledged or proved and certified. Any written instrument conveying real estate must also state whether each natural person acting as a grantor, mortgagor or other executing party is married or unmarried. Leaving out marital status is a common reason a recorder sends a deed back.

The recording statute adds a first-page checklist. Below a three-inch blank margin at the top, RSMo 59.310 expects the following:

  • the title of the document and its date;
  • every grantor's name and marital status;
  • every grantee's name;
  • any statutory addresses;
  • the legal description of the property;
  • book and page references where a statute calls for them.

If the first page lacks room, the page where the missing information appears must be stated there. Copy the legal description from your existing deed. A street address alone is not a legal description.

sections.h2: Where to record a Missouri quitclaim deed
sections.html:
The deed goes to the recorder of deeds for the county that holds the parcel. RSMo 442.380 directs an instrument that conveys real estate, once proved or acknowledged and certified in the prescribed manner, into the recorder's books in the county where the real estate lies.

State law also caps what a recorder may collect. Recording a deed or other instrument costs five dollars for page one and three dollars for each page after it. A certified or sealed copy and a plain copy have their own separate fees in the same statute. The recorder may add $25 when a document misses the format standards but is accepted anyway.

Some documents are exempt from the format rules, among them papers signed before January 1, 2002, certified copies and documents executed outside the United States. If a recorder rejects your deed, it must be returned to the preparer or presenter with an explanation. Ask whether the office takes documents electronically, because each recorder decides that for itself.

The format rules are detailed, and a recorder may turn a deed away for missing them. Under RSMo 59.310 the recorder can refuse a document that does not follow these:

  • one or more individual pages printed on one side only, not permanently bound and not in continuous form;
  • type no smaller than eight point, in black or dark ink;
  • white or light-colored paper of at least twenty-pound weight, free of watermarks;
  • signatures in black or dark ink, with the signer's name typed, printed or stamped beneath;
  • a top margin of at least three inches reserved for the recorder, and margins of at least three-fourths of an inch on every other side.

Nonessential items such as form numbers or customer notations may go in the margin. A document that is hard to read must come with an exact typed copy in eight-point type or larger. Staples that hold pages together are allowed, but avoid attachments unless a statute requires them.

sections.h2: What happens when a deed names more than one grantee?
sections.html:
The wording of the grantee clause decides how the new owners hold title. RSMo 442.450 makes an interest granted to two or more persons a tenancy in common unless the grant expressly declares joint tenancy. Executors and trustees and husband and wife are treated separately. A court annotation to that section shows how this can go wrong: a deed written by a layperson that used the phrase "tenants by entirety and to the survivor of them" for a mother and daughter was held to create a joint tenancy.

The lesson is to say what you mean in plain terms and avoid mixing labels. When siblings take an inherited house, tenancy in common is the default, and each co-owner can usually be asked to sign before a sale. If the intent is survivorship, the deed has to say so.

If the owner has died, a quitclaim from the heirs is not the only route. A deed that states it takes effect on the owner's death can be recorded during life under RSMo 461.025, and a small estate affidavit can be recorded afterward. Which one fits depends on facts a title company will want to see.

sections.h2: Risks of using a quitclaim deed in a sale
sections.html:
The risk comes less from the form itself and more from what is attached to the property and who signed. Missouri treats a false or forged deed seriously. Under RSMo 570.095, a person who files or presents a deed with intent to defraud, knowing it contains materially false information, is a forgery or lacks the consent of every party, commits the offense of filing false documents. A first offense is a class D felony, and the court must order restitution.

The same statute gives owners a remedy. Anyone who believes a recorded document is fraudulent can file a probable cause statement with the associate or circuit court serving the recording county. The first hearing must be set within twenty business days, and a ruling of invalid can be recorded at no filing fee.

For sellers, the sensible approach is to treat a quitclaim as one step in a title chain. Have the title company review the vesting deed, any lien and the proposed grantee before you sign, then send the finished deed to the recorder instead of holding it in a drawer. A cash buyer will run the same title check, so settling these points early shortens the closing.

faqs.q: Does a Missouri quitclaim deed need to be notarized?
faqs.a: It must be acknowledged or proved and certified. RSMo 442.130 requires the grantor, or a lawful agent, to sign, and the signature must be acknowledged in the manner the statute prescribes. Ask the recorder or your title company which officer can take the acknowledgment.

faqs.q: What will the recorder charge to file a Missouri deed?
faqs.a: The statutory charge is $5 for page one and $3 for every added page. A document that breaks the format rules but is accepted anyway carries a $25 surcharge. Ask the recorder about copy fees.

faqs.q: Do I have to state if the grantor is married?
faqs.a: Yes. Every written instrument conveying real estate must state whether each natural person signing as a grantor is married or unmarried, and the first page of a recorded document must show each grantor's name and marital status.

faqs.q: Which office files a Missouri deed?
faqs.a: The county recorder of deeds for the place the land is located. RSMo 442.380 sends instruments that convey real estate to that county's recorder.

faqs.q: What if two people receive property by one quitclaim deed?
faqs.a: They hold as tenants in common unless the deed expressly declares a joint tenancy. RSMo 442.450 makes that the rule for two or more grantees other than executors, trustees and husband and wife.
